name: Earth's field
description: Cathode-ray tubes had to be adjusted to how they stood in the Earth's magnetic field. Your electron beam must hit the detector whichever way the apparatus faces: no stray field, or a weak field in or out of the plane. Magnetic bending grows with the time spent in the field.

reality.represents: A cathode-ray tube's sensitivity to the Earth's magnetic field

remarks.line: Bending grows with the flight time
remarks.detail: A weak field bends the path as the square of the time spent in it, so slow particles over long paths are the most sensitive.

remarks.line: Only the field across the plane
remarks.detail: The Earth's field (about 50 µT, which moves a picture tube's beam by millimetres) also has parts along the tube, which would push the beam out of the plane; only the part across the plane is here.
Real tubes were corrected with small magnets and coils around the neck, or shielded; here charges do it.

Everything is symmetric about the plane z = 0, so the particle never leaves it. A real beam also has a width across the plane, where the same fields act differently (focusing in the plane can defocus across it).
